name: F3 · Threads Programming & Pthreads
description: Processes vs threads, execution models, synchronization concepts, Pthreads creation, mutexes, deadlocks, condition variables, R/W locks, attributes, cancellation, scheduling

cards.front: What is a process? What happens at a context switch and at fork()?
cards.back:
A **process** is a **program in execution**. It includes the program code and **all the data needed for the execution**: data on the runtime **stack** and the **heap**, the contents of the **registers**, etc.

- **Own address space:** processes do not share memory with each other.
- **Context switch:** the processor **changes from one process to another** by saving the state of the running process and loading the state of the next one.
  - **Multitasking** on one processor: processes take turns using **time slicing**. This is **concurrent but not parallel**.
  - **Multiprocessor systems:** processes really run at the same time, which is **true parallelism**.
- **Creation:** with the **`fork()`** call. The **child process gets a copy of the parent's address space** and continues with the **same program after the `fork` call**.
- **Rating:** creating and managing processes is **relatively time consuming** (copying the address space, kernel involvement, expensive context switches).

That cost, and the lack of shared memory, is why **threads** are used for parallel programming on multicore processors.

cards.front: What are threads, and what are their advantages over processes?
cards.back:
**Threads** extend the process model: **one process contains several independent flows of computation**. They are flows of computation **of the same program** that run in parallel and **access common variables in shared memory**.

**Advantages:**
- **Threads share the address space of their process**, so they can **exchange information quickly** by reading and writing shared variables (compared with e.g. sockets between processes).
- **Fast creation** of threads, since no address space needs to be copied.
- They can **execute on different processors/cores**, giving **true parallelism**.

**Each thread has its own:** program counter, registers and **runtime stack** (local variables).
**Shared by all threads of a process:** global data, the heap, program code, open files.

*Programming environments:* **Pthreads**, Java threads, OpenMP, Win32 threads.
*Drawback:* because everything is shared, **access to shared data must be synchronized**, or race conditions occur.

cards.front: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
cards.back:
**Concurrency:** several flows of computation are **in progress during the same period**, but not necessarily at the same instant. On **one processor** they take turns through **time slicing** (multitasking).

**Parallelism:** several computations **execute at literally the same time** on **different processors/cores**.

*Example:* two threads each summing half of an array.
- On **1 core** they are **concurrent**: the OS alternates between them every few milliseconds, and the total time is about the same as sequential.
- On **2 cores** they run **in parallel**, ideally finishing in half the time.

**Why it matters for synchronization:** the **effects of cooperation and coordination can differ** between concurrency and parallelism. A race condition can show up on a multicore machine even if it never appeared on a single core, because the interleavings are different and more frequent. A correct program must therefore be correct for **every possible interleaving**.

cards.front: What is the difference between user-level threads and OS-level (kernel) threads?
cards.back:
**User-level threads**
- Managed by a **thread library in user space**. **The OS has no knowledge of the threads**, only of the process.
- ✔ **Fast thread switching** and creation (no system call).
- ✘ If one thread makes a **blocking call** (e.g. waits for I/O), **the OS stops the whole process**, so **no switch to another thread** of that process is possible.
- ✘ The OS can't put the threads of one process on different processors, so there is **no true parallelism**.

**OS-level (kernel) threads**
- **Known to and scheduled by the operating system.**
- ✔ Different threads of one process can run **on different cores at the same time**.
- ✔ A blocking thread blocks **only itself**.
- ✘ Creation and switching are more expensive (kernel calls).

How user threads are mapped onto OS threads/processes gives the three **thread execution models**: **N:1, 1:1 and N:M**.

cards.front: Explain the N:1 thread execution model.
cards.back:
**N:1 mapping:** all the user threads (**N**) of a process are mapped by a **library scheduler** onto **one OS process (1)**. The **OS scheduler** then assigns OS processes to processors.

*In the figure:* the threads T of Process 1 go through the library scheduler to one OS process (BP), which the OS scheduler places on a processor P.

✔ **Very fast** thread creation and switching, entirely in user space with no kernel involvement.
✔ Works even if the OS doesn't support threads.

✘ **No true parallelism within a process:** the process runs on only **one processor** at a time, however many threads it has.
✘ **A blocking system call** (e.g. I/O) by one thread **blocks all the threads** of the process.

This is the **pure user-level thread** model, e.g. early "green threads" in Java. It is useless for speeding up a program on a multicore processor.

cards.front: Explain the 1:1 thread execution model.
cards.back:
**1:1 mapping:** **each user thread is mapped to its own OS thread** (BT). The **OS scheduler** assigns the OS threads directly to processors. There is no library scheduler.

*In the figure:* every T in Process 1 and Process n has its own arrow to an OS thread BT, and the OS scheduler maps the BTs to the processors P.

✔ **True parallelism:** the threads of one process can run on **different cores simultaneously**.
✔ A thread that **blocks** (I/O, waiting) **only blocks itself**, and the others keep running.
✔ Simple, because the OS does all the scheduling.

✘ Thread creation and switching need **kernel calls**, which is slower than pure user-level threads.
✘ Very many threads (e.g. 100 000) burden the OS.

**This is what Pthreads uses on Linux (NPTL) and Windows threads use**, so in the labs each `pthread_create` gives a real kernel thread that the OS can place on any core.

cards.front: Explain the N:M thread execution model.
cards.back:
**N:M mapping:** a **library scheduler** maps the **N user threads** of a process onto **M OS threads**, and the **OS scheduler** then maps the OS threads onto processors. It is **two-level scheduling**.

*In the figure:* the threads of each process go through a library scheduler to several BTs (OS threads), and the OS scheduler distributes the BTs over the processors.

✔ Combines the advantages: **cheap user-level switching** *and* **true parallelism** (M OS threads can run on M cores).
✔ Can support a huge number of light-weight threads (N ≫ M).
✔ A blocking thread can be handled by moving the other user threads to another OS thread.

✘ **Complex to implement**, and the two schedulers can make conflicting decisions (e.g. the library doesn't know when the OS deschedules an OS thread).

*Examples:* **Go goroutines** (many goroutines on a few OS threads), Java virtual threads, older Solaris threads. The Pthreads chapter's "library scheduler maps user threads to kernel threads" describes this model.

cards.front: What states can a thread be in, and what causes the transitions?
cards.back:
**States:** **New**, **Executable** (ready), **Running**, **Waiting** (blocked), **Finished**.

**Transitions:**
- **new → executable:** **start**. The thread is created and ready to run.
- **executable → running:** **assign**. The scheduler gives it a processor.
- **running → executable:** **interrupt**. Its time slice is over, or a higher-priority thread needs the processor.
- **running → waiting:** **block**. It waits for something, e.g. I/O, a locked mutex, or a condition variable.
- **waiting → executable:** **wakeup**. The event occurred (the mutex was released, another thread signalled the condition, the I/O finished).
- **running → finished:** **end**. The thread returns from its start function or calls `pthread_exit`.

**Note:** a woken-up thread goes back to **executable**, not straight to running. It has to be scheduled again first.

*Example:* a thread calls `pthread_mutex_lock` on a locked mutex: running → **waiting**. When the owner unlocks it: waiting → **executable** → (when scheduled) running.

cards.front: Which data is private to a thread and which is shared? How is the address space organized?
cards.back:
**Each thread has its own private runtime stack** for its **local data** (local variables, function parameters, return addresses):
- **Local data of a thread is invisible to the other threads.**
- The **stack exists as long as the thread exists**.
- So **special methods are required to pass a return value** (`pthread_exit(value)` / `pthread_join(tid, &value)`), because the thread's stack disappears when it ends.

**Shared by all threads:** **global data**, **heap data** (`malloc`), and the **program code**.

**Address space** (from high addresses to address 0):
- the stack region for the main thread, then for thread 1, thread 2, …
- the heap
- global data
- the program code

**Pitfall:** never return or pass on a pointer to a local variable of a thread that may already have ended. Its stack is gone. Use `malloc` or global data instead.

cards.front: What is synchronization of threads used for?
cards.back:
**Synchronization = coordination of threads.** It is used for:

1. **Getting a desired order of execution.** *E.g.* thread B may only use a result after thread A has computed it, or all threads must finish step k before anyone starts step k + 1.
2. **Designing the access to the shared memory.** *E.g.* only one thread at a time may update a shared counter or linked list.

**Why it's needed:**
- The **order in which computations execute determines the state of the shared memory**, i.e. which values end up in the shared variables.
- Synchronization **avoids undesired effects of parallel access** to a shared variable (lost updates, inconsistent data structures).
- The effects of cooperation and coordination **can differ between concurrency and parallelism**.

**Mechanisms covered:** barrier synchronization, locks (mutexes), condition variables, semaphores and monitors.

cards.front: What is barrier synchronization? Give an example where it's needed.
cards.back:
**Barrier synchronization:** **all participating threads wait for each other**, and **no thread executes an instruction after the synchronization point** until **every** thread has reached it.

**In Pthreads:**
```c
pthread_barrier_t b;
pthread_barrier_init(&b, NULL, NUM_THREADS);
...
for (k = 0; k < n; k++) {
    eliminate_my_rows(k);          // each thread: its part of step k
    pthread_barrier_wait(&b);      // wait until ALL threads are done with step k
}
```

*Example, Gaussian elimination (lab 1):* in step k every thread updates its rows using pivot row k. Step k + 1 uses rows that other threads changed in step k, so **no thread may start step k + 1 before everyone has finished step k**. A barrier after each step guarantees this.

*Also:* the `synch()` at the end of the shared-memory matrix-vector multiplication (F2) is a barrier, so no thread uses c before it is complete.

**Cost:** everyone waits for the **slowest** thread, so load imbalance shows up directly as waiting time.

cards.front: What is a race condition, a critical section and mutual exclusion?
cards.back:
**Race condition:** the **result of the parallel execution** of a program fragment by several threads **depends on the relative execution speed** of the threads. Executing it first by T1 and then T2 gives a **different result** than T2 first and then T1, so the behaviour is **non-deterministic**.

**Critical section:** a **program fragment with accesses to shared variables** that may also be **accessed concurrently by other threads**.
*Example:* `sum += a[i] * b[i];` where `sum` is shared.

**Mutual exclusion:** guarantees that **only one thread at a time** executes the critical section (accesses the variable exclusively). This gives a correct execution order and removes the race.
- *Methods:* **lock synchronization** (mutexes) and **condition variables**.

```c
pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
sum += local_sum;        // critical section: one thread at a time
pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
```

**Keep critical sections short.** Everything inside them runs sequentially.

cards.front: How do locks work? What happens when thread T1 calls lock(s)?
cards.back:
A **lock variable s** (or **mutex variable**) protects a critical region:
- **`lock(s)`** is called **before entering** the critical region.
- **`unlock(s)`** is called **after leaving** it.

**Effect of `lock(s)` for thread T1:**
- If **no other thread has locked s**, then s is **assigned to T1** (T1 becomes the owner) and T1 continues.
- If **another thread T2 has locked s**, then **T1 blocks until T2 releases s** by calling `unlock(s)`.

**Important:** race conditions are only avoided if **every** thread follows this convention. A lock does not physically protect the data. A thread that accesses the variable without locking still causes races.

**Realization:** in **Pthreads** (`pthread_mutex_lock` / `pthread_mutex_unlock`), **Java threads** (`synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`) and **OpenMP** (`omp_set_lock`, `#pragma omp critical`).

cards.front: What is a condition variable, conceptually?
cards.back:
With a **condition variable**, a thread **T1 blocks until a specific condition occurs**.
- **Waking up T1 can only be done by another thread T2** (by signalling the condition variable).
- **After waking up, T1 tests the condition again**, because it may have changed again (or not hold yet) when T1 gets to run.
- To **avoid race conditions**, an **additional lock (mutex) variable** is used together with the condition variable. It protects the variables in the condition.

*Example, producer-consumer:* a consumer waits on the condition "buffer not empty". When a producer inserts an item, it signals the condition variable, the consumer wakes up, re-checks that the buffer really is non-empty, and takes the item.

**Why not just loop and check?** That would be **busy waiting**: the thread uses CPU time doing nothing useful. A thread blocked on a condition variable uses **no CPU time** until it is woken.

cards.front: What is a semaphore? Explain P/wait and V/signal and the typical usage pattern.
cards.back:
A **semaphore** is a structure with an **integer counter s** that can only be accessed by **two atomic operations**:
- **P(s)** (or **wait(s)**): **waits until s > 0**, then **decrements s by 1** and continues.
- **V(s)** (or **signal(s)**): **increments s by 1**, which may let a waiting thread continue.

**Typical pattern** (with s initialized to 1):
```
wait(s)
critical section
signal(s)
```
With s = 1 it acts as a **lock** (a *binary semaphore*): the first thread brings s to 0, and the others wait.

**Counting semaphore:** with s initialized to **k**, **at most k threads** can be inside at the same time.
*Example:* a pool of 3 database connections. With s = 3, the 4th thread blocks in wait(s) until someone calls signal(s).

POSIX/C: `sem_t`, `sem_init`, `sem_wait`, `sem_post`.
**Unlike a mutex**, a semaphore has **no owner**: any thread may call signal. That makes it usable for signalling between threads too.

cards.front: What is a monitor?
cards.back:
A **monitor** is a **language construct** that **combines data and the operations that access that data into one structure**:
- The monitor data can **only be accessed through the monitor operations**.
- **Only one monitor operation may execute at a time**, so mutual exclusion is automatic.

✔ The programmer can't forget to lock: the **compiler/language enforces** the mutual exclusion.

*Example, Java:*
```java
class Counter {
    private int value;                          // data, only reachable via methods
    public synchronized void inc() { value++; }  // one thread at a time
    public synchronized int get()  { return value; }
}
```

**In C with Pthreads** there are no monitors, but you build the same thing by hand: a struct with the data **plus a mutex**, and functions that lock the mutex on entry and unlock it on exit. The thread-safe **linked list** (`list_t` with its own mutex, and `list_insert()`) is exactly this. Condition variables add the ability to wait inside the monitor.

cards.front: Compare locks, semaphores, condition variables, monitors and barriers.
cards.back:
| Mechanism | What it does | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Lock / mutex** | one thread at a time; has an **owner** who must unlock | protect a critical section |
| **Semaphore** | counter with atomic **P (wait)** / **V (signal)**, no owner | allow at most k threads; signal events |
| **Condition variable** | **block until a condition holds**; woken by another thread; used **with a mutex** | wait for "buffer not empty" |
| **Monitor** | **language construct**: data + operations, only one operation at a time | Java `synchronized` classes |
| **Barrier** | **all threads wait** until all have arrived | separate the phases of an iterative algorithm |

**Relations:**
- A binary semaphore (initialized to 1) can be used as a lock.
- A monitor = a lock that is taken automatically around every operation (+ condition variables for waiting).
- More complex mechanisms (e.g. **reader/writer locks**, barriers) can be **built from mutexes and condition variables**.

cards.front: How is a thread created with Pthreads? Explain the parameters of pthread_create.
cards.back:
When a Pthreads program starts, **one main thread** is active, executing `main()`. More threads are created with:

```c
int pthread_create(pthread_t *thread,
                   pthread_attr_t *attr,
                   void *(*start_routine)(void *),
                   void *arg);
```
- **`thread`:** receives the **thread ID** (TID) of the new thread, used later e.g. for `pthread_join`.
- **`attr`:** an **attribute object** for the thread's properties. **`NULL` gives the default properties.**
- **`start_routine`:** the **start function** that the new thread executes. It takes a `void *` and returns a `void *`.
- **`arg`:** **the parameter passed to the start function**.

**Note:** **only one parameter** can be passed to the start function, so **several parameters must be packed into a single structure** and a pointer to it passed as `arg`.

Returns 0 on success, or an error code.

cards.front: How does a Pthreads thread terminate, and how do you wait for it with pthread_join?
cards.back:
**Termination:**
```c
void pthread_exit(void *valuep);
```
- `valuep` = the **return value** handed to the thread that joins it.
- A thread also **terminates implicitly when it returns from its start function** (the returned pointer is the return value).

**Waiting for another thread:**
```c
int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **valuep);
```
- `thread` = the TID of the thread to wait for.
- `valuep` = where the **return value** is stored (or `NULL` if you don't need it).
- **Effect:** the calling thread is **blocked until the specified thread has terminated**.

**Only one thread can wait for the termination of a given thread.** If several call `pthread_join()` on it, only one call succeeds and the others return an error (**ESRCH** according to the slides).

```c
void *result;
pthread_join(tid, &result);   // blocks until tid is done
```
The return value must **not point to the thread's local variables**, because its stack is gone. Use `malloc` or global memory.

cards.front: How do you pass several parameters to a Pthreads thread? Why is pthread_join necessary in this example?
What race condition occurs when the same argument struct is passed to two threads, and how do you fix it?
Explain the Pthreads matrix multiplication with one thread per element of the result. What are its weaknesses?
cards.back:
**Idea:** for an 8 × 8 matrix product MC = MA · MB, **create one thread per element MC[r][c]**.

- Each thread gets its own `malloc`-ed **work struct** with `row`, `col` and pointers to MA, MB, MC (one struct per thread avoids the shared-argument race).
- The thread computes `MC[r][c] = Σᵢ MA[r][i] · MB[i][c]`.
- `main` creates **SIZE × SIZE = 64 threads** in a double loop, then joins all 64.

**Correct without locks:** every thread **writes a different element** MC[r][c], and MA and MB are **only read**, so there are no conflicting accesses.

**Weaknesses:**
- **Far too fine-grained:** each thread does only 8 multiply-adds, while creating and joining a thread costs much more. **64 threads on e.g. 4 cores** gives overhead and no benefit.
  → Better: **p threads, each computing a block of n/p rows**.
- The `work` structs are never `free`d (a memory leak).
- On the slide, `pthread_join(thread[row][col])` is **missing its second argument**. It should be `pthread_join(thread[row][col], NULL)`.

cards.front: Why do threads need coordination? Explain the scalar-product race, and how to fix it efficiently.
What is a Pthreads mutex variable, and what protocol guarantees mutual exclusion with it?
cards.back:
**Mutex variables** are data structures of type **`pthread_mutex_t`**, used to ensure **mutual exclusion**. A mutex is in one of two states: **locked** or **unlocked**.

**Protocol for protecting a shared data structure A:**
1. **Each data structure A** that can be accessed by several threads gets **its own mutex variable M_A**.
2. **Before every access to A (read or write)**, the thread **locks M_A**.
3. **After the access**, the thread **unlocks M_A**.

**Mutual exclusion is only guaranteed if every thread follows this procedure.** The mutex is just a convention. Nothing stops a thread from touching A without locking.

**Reads must also be locked:** otherwise a reader could see the structure **half-updated**, e.g. a linked list in the middle of an insert.

*Granularity choice:* one mutex for a whole list is simple but serializes all accesses. One mutex per element allows more parallelism but is more complex, with a risk of deadlock.

cards.front: How are Pthreads mutexes initialized, locked and unlocked? What happens to threads that wait for a locked mutex?
cards.back:
**Initialization** (before the first use):
```c
pthread_mutex_init(&m, NULL);                      // dynamic, NULL = default attributes
pthread_mutex_t m = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;      // static, with a macro
```

**Locking: `pthread_mutex_lock(&m)`**
- If m is **free**, it becomes **locked by the caller**, who continues.
- If m is **locked**, the caller is **blocked until the owner unlocks it**. **Waiting threads are organized in a queue.**

**Unlocking: `pthread_mutex_unlock(&m)`**
- If the **queue is empty**, m has **no owner** and becomes **free**.
- If the **queue is not empty**, **one waiting thread gets control of m** and is removed from the queue. **Which one is decided by priorities / the scheduling algorithm**, so it isn't necessarily the one that waited longest.

**Non-blocking attempt: `pthread_mutex_trylock(&m)`**
- If m is free, the caller **gets it** (returns 0).
- If m is locked, the call **fails immediately without blocking** and returns **EBUSY**.
- Useful e.g. for the back-off strategy against deadlocks, or to do other work instead of waiting.

cards.front: How is a thread-safe sorted linked list implemented with a mutex? Why must the whole search be inside the lock?
cards.back:
**Data structures:** the list holds its own mutex.
```c
typedef struct _node_t { int index; void *data; struct _node_t *next; } node_t;
typedef struct { node_t *first; pthread_mutex_t mutex; } list_t;
```
`list_init()` sets `first = NULL` and initializes the mutex.

**`list_insert(newindex, newdata, listp)`:**
1. `pthread_mutex_lock(&listp->mutex)`
2. **Walk the list** (`prev`, `curr`) until `curr->index >= newindex`
3. If the index is **not found**, `malloc` a new node and **link it in** between `prev` and `curr` (or first in the list)
4. `pthread_mutex_unlock(&listp->mutex)`

So **`list_insert()` is thread-safe**: any number of threads can call it concurrently.

**Why lock the search too?** The insert position is decided by the search. If another thread inserted or removed a node between our search and our insert, `prev`/`curr` would point to the wrong (or a freed) node, and the list would be corrupted.

**Trade-off:** one mutex for the whole list is simple and safe, but **all list operations are serialized**.

cards.front: How can a deadlock arise with two mutexes, and what are the two solutions?
cards.back:
**Deadlock example:** two mutexes `ma` and `mb`, and two threads:
```c
// T1                              // T2
pthread_mutex_lock(&ma);           pthread_mutex_lock(&mb);
pthread_mutex_lock(&mb);  // waits pthread_mutex_lock(&ma);  // waits
```
If **T1 is interrupted after locking ma**, and **T2 then locks mb**, each thread waits for the mutex the other holds, **forever**.

**Solution 1: locking hierarchy.** **Every thread locks the mutexes in the same order** (e.g. always ma before mb). Then a cycle of waiting threads is impossible.

**Solution 2: back-off strategy with `pthread_mutex_trylock()`.** Each thread may lock in its own order, but using trylock. **If an attempt fails, it unlocks every mutex it has locked so far (backs off)** and then **starts the whole locking procedure again**.
```c
for (;;) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&mb);
    if (pthread_mutex_trylock(&ma) == 0) break;   // got both
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&mb);                    // back off, retry
}
```
Since a thread never *waits* while holding a lock, there is no deadlock. (Repeated retries can waste time, though.)

cards.front: Why are condition variables needed? What is wrong with checking a condition repeatedly under a mutex?
cards.back:
Threads often have to **wait until a condition holds** before they can continue.
*Example, producer/consumer:* the **consumer** waits on an **empty buffer** until another thread puts in an item, and the **producer** waits on a **full buffer** until an item is removed.

**Mutex-only approach:** protect the variables in the condition with mutexes, and **from time to time** lock them, evaluate the condition, unlock, and try again later if it is false.
- ✘ The condition may have to be evaluated **very frequently**: **active (busy) waiting** **wastes CPU time** that other threads could use.

**Condition variable approach** (type `pthread_cond_t`), a **signalling mechanism**:
- If the condition is false, the thread **blocks on the condition variable**.
- As soon as the condition holds, **another thread wakes it up**.
- ✔ **No CPU time is used while waiting.**

**What it needs:**
1. a **condition variable**
2. a **mutex variable** assigned to the condition variable
3. a **condition** to evaluate, with **the evaluation protected by the mutex**

cards.front: What does pthread_cond_wait(&c, &m) do exactly?
cards.back:
**Before calling it,** the thread has **locked m** and tested the condition and found it false.

**`pthread_cond_wait(&c, &m)`:**
1. The calling thread **blocks, waiting on c**.
2. **At the same time, and atomically, it releases the mutex m.** Another thread can then lock m, change the condition and send a wake-up signal.
3. The thread is **only unblocked by a signal from another thread**. Without a signal it **stays blocked forever**.
4. **When woken up, it automatically tries to lock m again.** If m is taken, it blocks, waiting for m.
5. When the call returns, the thread **holds m again**.

**Why re-check the condition after waking?** While the thread was waiting to get m back, **another thread may have changed the variables in the condition** (e.g. another consumer took the item first). So the condition must be **re-evaluated** after `pthread_cond_wait` returns, which is why it is always called in a **`while`** loop.

**Initialization:** `pthread_cond_init(&c, NULL)` or `pthread_cond_t c = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;`

cards.front: What is the typical usage pattern for condition variables, and why is it a while loop and not an if?
What is the difference between pthread_cond_signal and pthread_cond_broadcast?
cards.back:
**`pthread_cond_signal(&c)`:** signals that the condition may have occurred.
- If **no thread is waiting** on c, it has **no effect** (the signal is not remembered).
- If threads are waiting, **one of them is woken up**, and it then tries to lock the associated mutex m.

**`pthread_cond_broadcast(&c)`:** wakes up **all** threads waiting on c.
- Each woken thread tries to lock m, but **at most one succeeds at a time**. The **others block on m** and get it one after another (each then re-checks its condition).

**When to use which:**
- **signal:** when **any one waiter can handle the event** and only one can proceed. *E.g.* one item was put in the buffer, so wake one consumer.
- **broadcast:** when **several waiters may be able to proceed**, or the waiters wait for **different conditions** on the same c. *E.g.* in the R/W lock, releasing a write lock lets **all waiting readers** in. Also when a barrier releases everyone.

Broadcast is always *safe* (thanks to the while loop) but may wake threads needlessly.

cards.front: Should pthread_cond_signal be called while holding the mutex or after unlocking it?
cards.back:
Calls to `pthread_cond_signal()` / `pthread_cond_broadcast()` should only be made **after the thread has evaluated (changed) the condition**, which requires **holding the mutex** for consistency.

The signal call itself **doesn't have to be protected by the mutex**, but each choice has a consequence:

**Signal while m is locked:**
- ✘ The woken thread **can't get m right away**. It blocks on m until the signaller unlocks (a small inefficiency).
- ✔ **Safe:** nothing can happen between changing the condition and signalling.

**Signal after unlocking m:**
- ✔ The woken thread may get m **directly**, without blocking on it.
- ✘ **This can lead to race conditions:** between the unlock and the signal, other threads can run. *Example:* another thread sees the condition already satisfied, finishes, and **destroys the condition variable** before the signal is sent.

**Rule of thumb:** change the condition, **signal while holding the mutex**, then unlock.

cards.front: In the numThreads example, SignalCond() decrements numThreads, unlocks the mutex and then signals. What can go wrong, and how is it fixed?
How can a signal be lost and cause a deadlock with condition variables? How is it avoided?
cards.back:
If **no thread is waiting** on c when `pthread_cond_signal(&c)` is called, the call **has no effect**, and the runtime system doesn't remember it: **the signal is lost**. If a thread then calls `pthread_cond_wait(&c)` and no further signal comes, it **stays blocked forever: deadlock**.

**Example:** SignalCond() sets the condition **without locking the mutex**:
```c
void SignalCond() {
    data.numThreads = 0;            // NOT protected by data.m
    pthread_cond_signal(&data.c);
}
```
**Problematic order** (numThreads > 0 at first):
1. T2 (WaitForCond) locks m, tests `numThreads > 0`, which is **true**, and is **interrupted before calling `pthread_cond_wait`**.
2. T1 sets numThreads = 0 and signals, but **T2 isn't waiting yet**, so the signal is lost.
3. T2 calls `pthread_cond_wait` and **waits forever**.

**Fix:** **change the variables of the condition only while holding data.m.** Then T1 can't run step 2 between T2's test and T2's wait. Since `pthread_cond_wait` releases m atomically, T1 gets m only once T2 is really waiting.

cards.front: What does pthread_cond_timedwait do?
Write a bounded buffer (producer-consumer) with a mutex and two condition variables.
What is a reader/writer lock, and how is it represented with Pthreads primitives?
How do rw_lock_rlock and rw_lock_wlock work?
How are read and write permissions released in the R/W lock, and why can writers starve?
Which models are used to organize the cooperation of threads in Pthreads programs?
cards.back:
- **Pipelining model:** an input/output relation between threads. **Thread Tᵢ gets the output of Tᵢ₋₁ as input** and produces data for Tᵢ₊₁. **After the start-up phase all the threads work in parallel** on different data items.
- **Master-Slave model:** a **master thread controls the execution** of the program, and the **slave threads perform the calculations** it assigns.
- **Worker model:** **equal worker threads** handle both the coordination and the calculations. There is no master.
  *Variation:* the calculations to be done are stored in **task pools**, and workers take tasks from the pool (and may add new ones).
- **Client-Server model:** **client threads generate requests**, and **server threads handle them** by performing the requested computations.

*Pthreads building blocks:* the task pool and pipeline buffers are shared data structures protected by **mutexes**, and threads wait for work with **condition variables** (producer-consumer).

cards.front: What are thread attribute objects in Pthreads, and what can they control?
cards.back:
So far `pthread_create()` was called with **`NULL`** as the attribute, giving **default threads**. The behaviour of threads can be changed with an **attribute object** of type `pthread_attr_t`:

```c
pthread_attr_t attr;
pthread_attr_init(&attr);                 // standard attribute values
/* change attributes with pthread_attr_set...() */
pthread_create(&tid, &attr, f, arg);
```

**What can be set (examples):**
- **Release of the return value** (detach state: joinable or detached)
- **Stack size** of the thread
- **Start address of the stack**
- **Termination (cancellation) behaviour**
- **Scheduling** (priority, method, contention scope)

The attributes must be set **before** `pthread_create`. Changing the attribute object afterwards doesn't affect threads that already exist.

cards.front: What is the detach state of a thread? Joinable vs detached.
cards.back:
The **detachstate** attribute decides what happens to a thread's **return value** when it ends.

**`PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE` (default):**
- The return value is assumed to be **needed after the thread terminates**, e.g. by `pthread_join()`.
- The runtime system **keeps the return value** (and thread information) in an internal structure **until some thread successfully calls `pthread_join()`** for it.
- A joinable thread that is never joined wastes resources (a "zombie" thread).

**`PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED`:**
- If the return value **won't be needed**, it is **freed immediately when the thread terminates**. **The thread can't be joined.**
```c
pthread_attr_setdetachstate(&attr, PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED);
```
- This must be set **before creating** the thread (setting it later has no effect).
- **An already running thread can be detached with `pthread_detach(tid)`.** This returns **EINVAL** if it is already detached.

*Use detached threads for "fire and forget" work*, e.g. a server thread handling one client request.

cards.front: How can a thread's stack size and stack address be set? What does the slide's attribute example do?
How can one thread cancel another in Pthreads, and what decides when the cancellation happens?
cards.back:
Threads can terminate each other, e.g. **when one detects that another's computation is redundant** (a parallel search where one thread has found the answer).
```c
int pthread_cancel(pthread_t tid);
```
This **starts** the termination of thread tid. **Returning from the call does not mean that tid has already terminated.**

**The behaviour depends on the target's cancellation state and type.** There are three modes:
1. **No interruptibility:** `pthread_setcancelstate(PTHREAD_CANCEL_DISABLE, &old)`. The request is **saved and executed later**, once the thread re-enables cancellation.
2. **Delayed (deferred) interruptibility:** the default (`PTHREAD_CANCEL_ENABLE`). The thread is terminated **when it reaches a cancellation point**.
3. **Direct (asynchronous) interruptibility:** the thread can be terminated **at any moment**.

**Why deferred is the default:** a thread killed at an arbitrary point could leave a **mutex locked** or a data structure half-updated. At a cancellation point the state is well-defined.

cards.front: What are cancellation points?
cards.back:
With deferred cancellation, a thread **checks for a pending cancellation request only at cancellation points**. If a request is there, **the thread terminates**.

**Obligatory cancellation points** (always), e.g. calls to:
- `pthread_cond_wait()`, `pthread_cond_timedwait()`, `pthread_join()`
- `pthread_testcancel()`
- `open()`, `read()`, `write()`, `wait()`

**Optional cancellation points** (implementation dependent): `printf()`, `fprintf()`, `scanf()`, `fscanf()`, `fopen()`, `fclose()`, etc.

**`pthread_testcancel()`** creates an **extra, user-defined cancellation point**. *Example:* a long computation loop without any blocking calls would never be cancelled, so insert one:
```c
for (i = 0; i < huge; i++) {
    compute(i);
    if (i % 1000 == 0) pthread_testcancel();   // allow cancellation here
}
```

cards.front: How are Pthreads scheduled, and which scheduling attributes can be influenced?
cards.back:
**Two levels:** the **user threads** defined by the programmer are mapped to **kernel threads** by the **library scheduler**, and the kernel threads are allocated to **processors** by the **operating system scheduler**.

The programmer can influence the library scheduler if **`_POSIX_THREAD_PRIORITY_SCHEDULING`** is defined (`<unistd.h>`) or `sysconf(_SC_THREAD_PRIORITY_SCHEDULING)` succeeds.

**Scheduling attributes** are stored in **`struct sched_param`** (`<sched.h>`), which has at least the entry **`int sched_priority`**.

**What can be influenced:**
- the **priority** of a thread: an integer within a range given by `sched_get_priority_min(policy)` / `sched_get_priority_max(policy)`
- the **scheduling method** (policy)
- the **contention scope**: **process** scope (the thread competes only with threads of its own process) or **global/system** scope (it competes with all threads in the system)

cards.front: How does the Pthreads priority scheduler work? Which scheduling methods exist, and how is a priority set?
cards.back:
**Operation:**
- The library scheduler keeps **one queue per priority** with all the ready threads of that priority.
- To run a new thread, it **picks from the non-empty queue with the highest priority**.
- **Within a queue**, the **scheduling method** decides which thread goes next.
- **Effect:** **low-priority threads may starve**, since the highest priorities always run first.

**At least 32 priority levels** must be available.

**Scheduling methods** (for threads of the same priority):
1. **SCHED_FIFO:** first-in-first-out. A thread runs until it blocks or finishes.
2. **SCHED_RR:** **round robin**. Like FIFO, but with time slices, so threads take turns.
3. **SCHED_OTHER:** implementation-specific (e.g. the normal time-sharing scheduler).
The standard **doesn't specify a default** method.

**Setting a priority:**
```c
struct sched_param sp;
sp.sched_priority = 10;
pthread_attr_setschedparam(&attr, &sp);
pthread_create(&tid, &attr, f, arg);
```
(`pthread_attr_getschedparam` reads it back.)

cards.front: How do you make sure that an initialization is executed exactly once? Explain pthread_once.
cards.back:
Sometimes a task (e.g. **initializing a data structure**) must run **exactly once**, but it isn't known in advance **which thread** will get there first.

**Simple solution:** a **boolean flag, initially FALSE, protected by a mutex**. The first thread to arrive locks the mutex, sees FALSE, sets it to TRUE and performs the task. Later threads see TRUE and skip it.

**Pthreads solution: `pthread_once`**
```c
pthread_once_t once = PTHREAD_ONCE_INIT;    // control variable
void init_routine(void) { /* the one-time task, no parameters */ }
...
pthread_once(&once, init_routine);          // may be called by many threads
```
**Effect:**
- **Only the first call** executes `init_routine()`.
- If another thread is **currently executing** `init_routine()`, a caller **waits until it has finished**.
- If it has **already finished**, the call **returns immediately**.

So after `pthread_once` returns, the initialization is **guaranteed to be complete**.
